danish.title: Femte bog (1806–07) — Kapitel 17
paragraphs: I juni blev Friedland-slaget udkæmpet, hvori Pavlograderne ikke deltog, og derefter blev der erklæret våbenstilstand. Rostov, der savnede sin ven meget og ikke havde hørt fra ham, siden han tog af sted, og som var meget bekymret for hans sår og hans sags forløb, benyttede våbenstilstanden til at få orlov og besøge Denisov på hospitalet.

Hospitalet lå i en lille preussisk by, der to gange var blevet ødelagt af russiske og franske tropper. Fordi det var sommer, og alt var så smukt ude på markerne, frembød den lille by med sine knuste tage og hegn, snavsede gader, lasede beboere og syge og berusede soldater, der vandrede omkring, et særligt trist billede.

Hospitalet lå i en murstensbygning, hvor nogle vinduesrammer og ruder var knust, og med en gård omgivet af resterne af et træhegn, der var revet fra hinanden. Adskillige forbundne soldater med blege, opsvulmede ansigter sad eller gik omkring i solskinnet i gården.

Straks Rostov trådte ind ad døren, blev han indhyllet af en lugt af forrådnelse og hospitalsluft. På trappen mødte han en russisk militærlæge, der røg en cigar. Lægen blev fulgt af en russisk assistent.
»Jeg kan ikke flå mig selv i stykker,« sagde lægen. »Kom til Makar Aleksejevitj i aften. Jeg skal være dér.«
Assistenten stillede nogle flere spørgsmål.
»Åh, gør det bedste, du kan! Er det ikke lige meget?« Lægen lagde mærke til Rostov, der kom op ad trappen.
»Hvad ønsker De, hr?« sagde lægen. »Hvad ønsker De? Har kuglerne skånet Dem, og vil De nu prøve tyfus? Det her er en pestbolig, hr.«
»Hvordan det?« spurgte Rostov.

»Tyfus, hr. Det er den visse død at gå derind. Kun vi to, Makejev og jeg« — han pegede på assistenten — »holder ud herinde. Fem af os læger er døde her allerede... Når en ny kommer, er han færdig inden en uge,« sagde lægen med synlig tilfredsstillelse. »Preussiske læger er blevet inviteret herhen, men vores allierede bryder sig slet ikke om det.«
Rostov forklarede, at han ønskede at se major Denisov fra husarerne, som var såret.

»Det ved jeg ikke. Jeg kan ikke sige Dem det, hr. Tænk bare! Jeg er alene om ansvaret for tre hospitaler med over fire hundrede patienter! Det er heldigt, at de velgørende preussiske damer sender os to pund kaffe og noget charpi hver måned, ellers var vi fortabte!« han lo. »Fire hundrede, hr, og de sender mig hele tiden nye. Der er fire hundrede, ikke? Hva'?« spurgte han og vendte sig mod assistenten.
Assistenten så udkørt ud. Han var tydeligvis irriteret og utålmodig efter, at den snakkesalige læge skulle gå.
»Major Denisov,« sagde Rostov igen. »Han blev såret ved Molliten.«
»Død, tror jeg. Hva', Makejev?« spurgte lægen i en ligegyldig tone.
Assistenten bekræftede dog ikke lægens ord.
»Er han høj og med rødligt hår?« spurgte lægen.
Rostov beskrev Denisovs udseende.
»Der var én, der så sådan ud,« sagde lægen, som om det glædede ham. »Den er død, tror jeg. Men jeg skal slå op i vores liste. Vi havde en liste. Har du den, Makejev?«
»Makar Aleksejevitj har listen,« svarede assistenten. »Men hvis De vil gå ind på officersafdelingen, kan De selv se efter,« tilføjede han henvendt til Rostov.
»Åh, det ville jeg ikke gøre, hr,« sagde lægen, »ellers risikerer De selv at måtte blive her.«
Men Rostov takkede og bad assistenten vise ham vej.
»Giv bare ikke mig skylden!« råbte lægen efter ham op ad trappen.

Rostov og assistenten gik ud i den mørke korridor. Lugten var så stærk der, at Rostov holdt sig for næsen og måtte standse et øjeblik for at samle kræfter, før han kunne gå videre. En dør gik op til højre, og en udmagret, gulbleg mand på krykker, barfodet og i undertøj, humpede ud og lænede sig mod dørkarmen, mens han med glødende, misundelige øjne kiggede på dem, der gik forbi. Da Rostov kiggede ind ad døren, så han, at de syge og sårede lå på gulvet på halm og kapper.
»Må jeg gå ind og se?«
»Hvad er der at se?« sagde assistenten.

Men netop fordi assistenten tydeligvis ikke ønskede, at han gik derind, trådte Rostov ind på soldaterstuen. Den fæle luft, som han allerede var begyndt at vænne sig til i korridoren, var endnu stærkere her. Den var lidt anderledes, mere skarp, og man følte, at det var herfra, den stammede.

I det lange rum, klart oplyst af solen gennem de store vinduer, lå de syge og sårede i to rækker med hovederne mod væggene og med en passage i midten. De fleste var bevidstløse og lagde ikke mærke til de nyankomne. De, der var ved bevidsthed, rejste sig op eller løftede deres tynde, gule ansigter, og alle stirrede indtrængende på Rostov med det samme udtryk af håb, lettelse, bebrejdelse og misundelse over en andens sundhed. Rostov gik til midten af rummet og kiggede gennem de åbne døre ind i de to tilstødende rum og så det samme dér. Han blev stående og så tavst sig om. Han havde slet ikke ventet et sådant syn. Lige foran ham, næsten tværs over midterpassagen på det bare gulv, lå en syg mand, formentlig en kosak at dømme efter hans frisure. Manden lå på ryggen med sine enorme arme og ben strakt ud. Hans ansigt var violet, hans øjne var rullet tilbage, så kun det hvide var synligt, og på hans bare ben og arme, der stadig var røde, stod venerne frem som reb. Han bankede baghovedet mod gulvet og stønnede hæst et ord igen og igen. Rostov lyttede og tydede ordet. Det var »drik, drik, noget at drikke!« Rostov så sig om efter nogen, der kunne lægge denne mand på plads og give ham vand.
»Hvem passer de syge her?« spurgte han assistenten.
Lige da kom en soldat fra intendanturen, en hospitalsordonnans, ind fra det næste rum, marcherede stift hen og stillede sig op foran Rostov.
»Goddag, Deres velbyrdighed!« råbte han og rullede med øjnene mod Rostov, idet han tydeligvis forvekslede ham med en af hospitalets autoriteter.
»Læg ham på plads og giv ham noget vand,« sagde Rostov og pegede på kosakken.
»Ja, Deres velbyrdighed,« svarede soldaten underdanigt og rullede mere end nogensinde med øjnene, rettede sig yderligere i stilling, men rørte sig ikke.

»Nej, her kan man intet gøre,« tænkte Rostov og sænkede blikket. Han var ved at gå, men blev opmærksom på et indtrængende blik, der var rettet mod ham fra højre, og han drejede sig om. Tæt ved hjørnet, på en kappe, sad en gammel, ubarberet, gråskægget soldat, tynd som et skelet, med et strengt, gulblegt ansigt og øjne fast rettet mod Rostov. Mandens nabo på den ene side hviskede noget til ham og pegede på Rostov, som opdagede, at den gamle mand gerne ville tale med ham. Han gik nærmere og så, at den gamle kun havde ét ben bøjet under sig, det andet var amputeret over knæet. Hans nabo på den anden side, der lå ubevægeligt et stykke derfra med hovedet kastet bagover, var en ung soldat med en stumpnæse. Hans blege, voksagtige ansigt var stadig fregnet, og hans øjne var rullet tilbage. Rostov så på den unge soldat, og et koldt gys løb ham ned ad ryggen.
»Jamen, den her ser ud til at...« begyndte han og vendte sig mod assistenten.
»Åh, og vi har bedt og bedt, Deres velbyrdighed,« sagde den gamle soldat med skælvende kæbe. »Han har været død siden i morges. Vi er trods alt mennesker, ikke hunde.«
»Jeg sender nogen straks. Han skal flyttes — flyttes med det samme,« sagde assistenten hastigt. »Lad os gå, Deres velbyrdighed.«

»Ja, ja, lad os gå,« sagde Rostov i hast, og med sænket blik og krybende sammen forsøgte han at passere ubemærket mellem rækkerne af bebrejdende, misundelige øjne, der var rettet mod ham, og gik ud af stuen.

english.title: Book Five (1806 - 07) — Chapter 17
paragraphs: In June the Battle of Friedland was fought, in which the Pavlograds took no part, and afterward an armistice was declared. Rostov, who felt his friend's absence keenly, having had no news of him since he left and being very anxious about his wound and his legal troubles, took advantage of the armistice to get leave and visit Denisov in the hospital.

The hospital was in a small Prussian town that had been devastated twice by Russian and French troops. Because it was summer, when everything is so beautiful outdoors, the little town looked especially dismal with its broken roofs and fences, its filthy streets, its ragged inhabitants, and the sick and drunken soldiers wandering about.

The hospital occupied a brick building with some of its window frames and panes broken, surrounded by a courtyard enclosed by the remnants of a wooden fence that had been torn apart. Several bandaged soldiers with pale, swollen faces were sitting or walking about in the sunshine in the yard.

The moment Rostov entered the building, he was enveloped by a smell of decay and the stale air of a hospital. On the stairs he met a Russian army doctor smoking a cigar, followed by a Russian assistant.
"I can't tear myself in half," the doctor was saying. "Come to Makar Alexeevich's this evening. I'll be there."
The assistant asked some more questions.
"Oh, do the best you can! What difference does it make?" The doctor noticed Rostov coming up the stairs.
"What do you want, sir?" said the doctor. "What do you want? The bullets spared you — are you here to catch typhus? This place is a death trap, sir."
"How so?" asked Rostov.

"Typhus, sir. Anyone who comes in here dies. Only the two of us — Makeev and I" — he pointed at the assistant — "are still standing. Five doctors have died in this place already. When a new one arrives, he's finished within a week," said the doctor with obvious pride. "Prussian doctors have been invited, but our allies don't care for it at all."
Rostov explained that he wanted to see Major Denisov of the hussars, who had been wounded.

"I have no idea — I can't tell you, sir. Just think! I'm alone in charge of three hospitals with over four hundred patients! It's a good thing the charitable Prussian ladies send us two pounds of coffee and some lint each month, or we'd be done for!" he laughed. "Four hundred, sir, and they keep sending me fresh ones. There are four hundred, aren't there?" he asked, turning to the assistant.
The assistant looked exhausted — clearly irritated and waiting for the chatty doctor to leave.
"Major Denisov," Rostov said again. "He was wounded at Molliten."
"Dead, I think. Eh, Makeev?" the doctor asked indifferently.
The assistant, however, did not confirm the doctor's words.
"Is he tall and with reddish hair?" asked the doctor.
Rostov described Denisov's appearance.
"There was one like that," said the doctor, sounding pleased. "That one's dead, I think. But I'll check our list. We had a list. Do you have it, Makeev?"
"Makar Alexeevich has the list," the assistant answered. "But if you go to the officers' ward, you'll see for yourself," he added, turning to Rostov.
"Better not, sir," said the doctor. "You might end up staying here yourself."
But Rostov politely excused himself from the doctor and asked the assistant to show him the way.
"Just don't blame me!" the doctor shouted after him.

Rostov and the assistant entered the dark corridor. The smell was so overpowering there that Rostov had to hold his nose and stop to gather himself before going on. A door opened on the right, and a gaunt, sallow man on crutches — barefoot, wearing only his underclothes — limped out and, leaning against the doorframe, stared with glittering, envious eyes at the people passing by. Glancing through the door, Rostov saw sick and wounded men lying on the floor on straw and overcoats.
"May I go in and look?"
"What's there to see?" said the assistant.

But precisely because the assistant obviously didn't want him to go in, Rostov entered the soldiers' ward. The foul air, which he'd already started getting used to in the corridor, was even stronger here — different, more acrid — and one could tell this was where it originated.

In the long room, brightly lit by sun through the large windows, the sick and wounded lay in two rows with their heads against the walls, leaving a passage down the middle. Most were unconscious and took no notice of the visitors. Those who were awake raised themselves or lifted their thin, yellow faces, all staring at Rostov with the same expression — hope, relief, reproach, and envy of someone else's health. Rostov walked to the center of the room and through the open doors saw the same scene in the two rooms beyond. He stopped and looked around in silence. He had not expected anything like this. Right in front of him, almost blocking the passage on the bare floor, lay a sick man — probably a Cossack, judging by his haircut. The man lay on his back, his massive arms and legs stretched out. His face was purple, his eyes rolled back until only the whites showed, and on his bare legs and arms — still red — the veins stood out like cords. He was knocking the back of his head against the floor, hoarsely repeating a single word over and over. Rostov listened and made it out. It was: "Drink... drink... a drink!" Rostov looked around for someone to help this man back to his place and bring him water.
"Who looks after the sick here?" he asked the assistant.
Just then a commissariat soldier — a hospital orderly — marched stiffly in from the next room and drew himself up in front of Rostov.
"Good day, your honor!" he shouted, rolling his eyes at Rostov, evidently taking him for a hospital official.
"Get this man to his place and bring him water," said Rostov, pointing to the Cossack.
"Yes, your honor," the soldier replied with gusto, rolling his eyes even more and standing even straighter — but not moving.

"No — nothing can be done here," thought Rostov, lowering his eyes. He was about to leave when he became aware of an intense gaze fixed on him from the right. He turned. Near the corner, sitting on an overcoat, was an old, unshaven, gray-bearded soldier, thin as a skeleton, with a stern sallow face and eyes locked on Rostov. The man's neighbor on one side was whispering something to him, pointing at Rostov. The old man clearly wanted to speak. Rostov moved closer and saw that the man had only one leg bent beneath him — the other had been amputated above the knee. His neighbor on the other side, who lay motionless at some distance with his head thrown back, was a young soldier with a snub nose. His pale, waxy face was still freckled, and his eyes were rolled back. Rostov looked at the young soldier and felt a cold chill run down his spine.
"Why, this one seems..." he began, turning to the assistant.
"We've been begging and begging, your honor," said the old soldier, his jaw trembling. "He's been dead since this morning. We're men after all, not dogs."
"I'll send someone right away. He'll be removed — removed immediately," said the assistant quickly. "Let's go, your honor."
"Yes, yes, let's go," said Rostov hastily, and with lowered eyes, trying to make himself invisible, he hurried between the rows of reproachful, envious eyes fixed on him, and escaped from the room.
